kurz: How to determine your needs in retirement from your expenses rather than from your last paycheck, and how to derive the gap above Social Security and the capital requirement from them.

bloecke.md:
The question of how much money you need in retirement is almost always approached from the income side. This calculation shows how much Social Security and pension income will result, but says nothing about whether the amount is enough. The reverse order is more informative. First the requirement is determined, then the secured income is established. The difference is the amount that your savings have to cover.

Three quantities are enough for this, namely the monthly spending need in retirement, the monthly income from all lifelong sources after Medicare premiums and taxes, and the capital that funds the difference over twenty to thirty-five years. Further details merely refine the calculation.

## Expenses that end and new expenses

Your last paycheck is a poor yardstick, because it contains items that disappear with your last working day. Payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare (7.65% of wages for employees) end, and so do your 401(k) contributions and any other saving for retirement. In addition, there are work-related costs such as commuting, a second car, lunches out, work clothing and further training. In many households, the mortgage is paid off by then, and the costs of children run out.

Other expenses rise. Medicare has premiums, deductibles and coinsurance, and it does not cover dental care, routine vision care or hearing aids. Later, help in the household and changes to the home may be needed. In the first years of retirement, there is often additional spending on travel and on purchases for which there was previously no time. Studies of spending patterns in retirement typically find a U-shape. Spending is high at the beginning and at the end and lower in the years in between. The average is suitable as a planning figure, but it is not sufficient for liquidity planning.

bloecke.formel: Spending need = take-home pay − saving from take-home pay − work-related costs − mortgage payment that ends + new expenses
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula replaces the rule of thumb with four items that can be read from your own bank statements. Payroll taxes and 401(k) contributions are already deducted from take-home pay. The personal replacement rate follows as a result and does not have to be assumed.
variablen: monthly net pay of the household in the last year of work
IRA contributions, brokerage savings plans and other regular saving
commuting, meals, clothing, professional dues, a second car
Medicare premiums except Part B, out-of-pocket health costs, travel, help in the household
bloecke.beispiel: $4,100 take-home pay − $300 saving − $200 work-related costs − $600 mortgage payment that ends + $300 new expenses = $3,300 need, that is, 80% of take-home pay.

bloecke.md:
## Replacement rate and Social Security

The [[Replacement rate|replacement rate]] is retirement income divided by previous income. Its value depends entirely on which two figures you use. The Social Security Administration states that benefits replace about 40% of pre-retirement earnings for an average earner. That figure refers to gross earnings and a worker with average wages throughout; it says nothing about any individual person.

The benefit formula is progressive. The primary insurance amount (PIA), the benefit at full retirement age, is calculated from your average indexed monthly earnings (AIME) over your 35 highest-earning years. For workers who turn 62 in 2026, it is 90% of the first $1,286 of AIME, 32% of the amount up to $7,749 and 15% above that. Low earners therefore get a much higher replacement rate than high earners. The widespread rules of thumb of 70% to 80% of pre-retirement income do not apply generally either. They result mainly from the savings rate and payroll taxes, which no longer apply. The ratio is therefore a result of the calculation and not an input.

bloecke.titel: The most common misconception about the 40%
bloecke.md: The 40% does not mean that you will receive 40% of your last salary. It applies to a worker with average earnings over a full career. For people who most recently earned well above average, the personal ratio is far lower, because the 15% factor applies to earnings above the second bend point and earnings above the taxable maximum ($184,500 in 2026) do not count at all. A career with a steep rise towards the end reinforces this, because the formula averages 35 years, and early years with low earnings, or years with no earnings, remain in the average.

## From gross benefit to spendable income

The standard Medicare Part B premium is deducted directly from the Social Security payment. In 2026 it is $202.90 a month; with higher incomes, an income-related surcharge is added. Most retirees also pay premiums for drug coverage (Part D) and for a Medigap policy or a Medicare Advantage plan. These premiums are not deducted automatically, but they are fixed costs that only arise in retirement.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 86, up to 85% of Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. What counts is provisional income: your other income plus half of the benefits. Below $25,000 for single filers and $32,000 for married couples filing jointly, no benefits are taxable; above $34,000 and $44,000, up to 85% are. These thresholds have never been adjusted for inflation. If Social Security is your only income, it usually remains tax-free. Withdrawals from a traditional 401(k) or IRA, by contrast, are fully taxable and can make part of the benefits taxable as well. Most states do not tax Social Security benefits; a minority of states do, under their own rules.

bloecke.titel: From a gross benefit of $2,665.80 to spendable income
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for an AIME of $6,000, claiming at full retirement age and no other income; the Part D and Medigap premiums are assumptions, as they vary by plan, state and age.

bloecke.titel: Three earnings histories, each with 35 years of earnings

bloecke.md: The benefits are calculated with the 2026 bend points of $1,286 and $7,749 and expressed in 2026 dollars. The real benefit is calculated in the year you turn 62 and then rises with the annual cost-of-living adjustment. Only the Part B premium is deducted. With Social Security as the only income, none of the three cases owes federal income tax on the benefits. The ratio of benefit to earnings is 51% in case A, 44% in case B and 38% in case C. Your own estimate is in your Social Security Statement at ssa.gov/myaccount, already expressed in today's dollars.

## Inflation over thirty years

A retirement extends over two to three and a half decades. Over this period, the loss of purchasing power is the largest single item. The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% over the longer run. At this target, the purchasing power of $1,500 falls to $828 in thirty years. At 3%, it is $618, just under 59% less than at the start.

Social Security, by contrast, is not a fixed amount. Benefits are adjusted every January by the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), which follows the consumer price index for urban wage earners (CPI-W); for 2026 it is 2.8%. Whether this index reflects the spending of retirees well is disputed, but the link to prices is direct. Most private pensions from former employers and most private income annuities, by contrast, are fixed in nominal terms. A careful calculation of needs therefore has to include the question of which part of future income is adjusted for inflation and which remains fixed.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation of the purchasing power of a nominally fixed amount from the start of retirement in 2026 at constant inflation of 2% or 3%.

bloecke.md:
## From the gap to the capital requirement

Once the spending need and the secured income are known, a monthly gap results. A capital stock has to cover this gap over the entire duration of retirement. The methodologically sound approach is to calculate via the present value of an annuity. You calculate in today's purchasing power and apply a **real return**, that is, the return after inflation. A calculation with nominal returns that ignores inflation considerably overestimates how long the capital will last. If the capital sits in a traditional 401(k) or IRA, the withdrawals are taxable, and the gap has to be grossed up by the expected tax.

The range of assumptions matters more than the decimal places. For a broadly diversified portfolio of stocks and bonds, a real return of 2% in the withdrawal phase is a cautious assumption. A real return of 0% means that the assets are simply used up. The results show immediately how strongly each assumption affects the outcome. A withdrawal period five years longer increases the capital requirement by about as much as one percentage point less return.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula calculates the present value of an annuity paid in arrears over n years at a real return r. At r = 0, the factor simplifies to n. The factor states how many annual amounts of capital are needed.
variablen: real return after inflation, as a decimal
planned duration of withdrawals in years

bloecke.titel: Capital requirement for a monthly gap of $1,000
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in thousands of dollars and today's purchasing power, in which five more years of withdrawals have a similar effect to one percentage point less return.

bloecke.titel: Need, gap and capital for the three cases

bloecke.md: During working life, case A and case C are $60,000 of indexed earnings a year apart, but only about $110,000 apart in capital requirement. The benefit grows much less than proportionally with earnings, because the formula is progressive. The need, however, also grows less than proportionally, because households with higher incomes typically saved more and had more work-related costs. It follows that, relative to income, the capital requirement is hardest to raise for lower incomes. In case A it corresponds to more than four years of earnings, in case C to about three. In addition, the capital in a traditional 401(k) or IRA has to cover the income tax on the withdrawals, which is higher in case C.

Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care, that is, help with daily activities such as bathing, dressing and eating, in a nursing home or at home. Recent national cost surveys put a year in a nursing home well above $100,000, and costs differ considerably by state and region. That is too much to plan for as a monthly item, and a long stay in a nursing home is too uncertain to assume. In planning, long-term care costs are therefore treated as a risk at the end of life and covered by a reserve, by home equity as a last resort or by insurance. Medicaid pays only once income and assets have largely been used up. Details are covered in the separate lesson on long-term care and health insurance.

Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicaid are means-tested. For SSI, countable resources may not exceed $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple, limits that have not been raised since 1989, and almost every dollar of other income above small disregards reduces the benefit. Many states use similar limits for Medicaid long-term care. Retirement savings can therefore count against eligibility. For households with very low earnings, Social Security already replaces a large share of income, and money saved may later partly replace benefits that would otherwise have been paid. The calculation of needs must show this openly; it is not an argument against an emergency fund.

Two measures have a stronger effect than the savings contribution.

Claiming Social Security later raises the benefit for life. For people born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67. Claiming at 62 reduces the benefit by 30%; each year of delay after full retirement age raises it by 8%, up to age 70, when it is 124% of the PIA. In case B, the benefit at 70 is $3,305.59 instead of $2,665.80. The gap after Part B then shrinks from about $840 to about $200 a month, while the portfolio has to bridge three years of about $3,300 a month. In total, the capital requirement falls from about $225,000 to about $160,000.

The second measure is working part-time. Before full retirement age, the earnings test withholds $1 of benefits for every $2 earned above $24,480 a year in 2026 (and $1 for every $3 above $65,160 in the year you reach full retirement age); the withheld benefits are credited later through a higher benefit. From full retirement age on, there is no limit. Additional net earnings of $500 a month over five years replace around $28,000 of capital in arithmetical terms.

The target figure is made up of four components: spending need in today's purchasing power, income from all lifelong sources after Medicare premiums and taxes, assumed withdrawal period and real return. A percentage of your last salary does not replace this calculation. If one of the components changes, the result changes, and duration, return and need have effects of a similar order of magnitude.

The starting point is case B with a gap of about $840, 30 years and a real return of 2%, which requires around $225,000 of capital.

- With a withdrawal period of 35 instead of 30 years, the capital rises to around $251,000, that is, by 12%.
- With a real return of 1% instead of 2%, the factor rises from 22.40 to 25.81 and the capital to around $259,000.
- With a need 5% lower ($165 a month), the capital falls to around $181,000, that is, by around $44,000.

The last point is often underestimated. Because Social Security covers most of the need, a spending base that is permanently 5% lower reduces the gap by a fifth and has a stronger effect here than one percentage point of return. It is the only one of the three quantities that you decide on yourself.

mitnehmen: The need in retirement is derived from take-home pay less saving, work-related costs and payments that end, and not from a rule of thumb.
The 40% replacement rate of Social Security applies to an average earner over a full career; because the formula is progressive, higher earners receive far less in relation to their earnings.
The Part B premium of $202.90 (2026) is deducted from the benefit, up to 85% of benefits can be taxable depending on other income, and the COLA links Social Security to consumer prices.
The gap is converted into a capital requirement via the present value of an annuity, using the formula monthly gap × 12 × factor at a real return.
Claiming Social Security later and a lower spending base reduce the capital requirement more than a higher return; long-term care is planned as a risk at the end of life and not as a monthly item.

begriffe.text: Ratio of income in retirement to income before retirement. It is only meaningful if both reference figures are named, gross or net. The roughly 40% that Social Security replaces for an average earner is not a personal replacement rate.

Monthly Social Security benefit at full retirement age. It is calculated from the average indexed monthly earnings with a progressive formula of 90%, 32% and 15% between two bend points. Claiming earlier reduces it, claiming later up to age 70 increases it.
Average of the 35 highest years of earnings subject to Social Security tax, indexed to wage growth up to age 60 and divided by 420 months. Years without earnings count as zero.
Number of annual amounts needed as capital to fund a withdrawal over n years at a real return r. The factor is (1 − (1 + r)^−n) / r.
Return after deducting inflation. If need and capital are stated in today's purchasing power, only this return may be used in the calculation.
